newsitem.title: UK: UK media could swing election result - study.
newsitem.headline: UK media could swing election result - study.

text.p: British newspaper coverage of the main political parties in the run up to May 1 elections will play a direct role in swaying voters as the campaign gathers pace, according to a new study.
But with national papers deserting the ruling Conservatives in droves, this may prove to be good news for the opposition Labour Party for the first time in more than 20 years.

Media analysis firm Carma International said on Friday it expected to see the trend in opinion polls -- which predict a landslide victory for the main opposition Labour Party -- to be heavily influenced by the slant of press coverage over the next four weeks.

"We expect to see a very strong correlation between the two," said Claire Spencer, consultant for Carma. "Labour are doing well because they've been able to focus on positive issues like the economy and education whereas the sleaze issue has dominated coverage of the Conservatives."
Unlike any other election since 1979, the importance of newspaper coverage may not be bad news for Labour this time.
Traditionally, most of Britain's national newspapers -- both broadsheet and tabloid -- have lined up behind the Conservatives at election time, producing reams of anti-Labour copy.

In 1992, the mass-circulation Sun newspaper claimed "It was the Sun Wot Won It" for John Major's Conservatives. On the day of the election its front page asked the last person leaving Britain to turn out the lights if Neil Kinnock, Labour's then leader, took power.

But now The Sun has come out in favour of Labour leader Tony Blair and even died-in-the-wool Conservative papers like the Daily Telegraph have found it tough to get excited about Prime Minister John Major and his ruling party.

The main opposition Labour Party, which has shrugged off its socialist tax-and-spend' image for a more centrist position under Tony Blair, is racing ahead in polls and looks set to end 18 years of Conservative rule. The latest surveys give Labour a lead of more than 20 points.
Carma showed British newspapers almost unanimously favoured Labour over the Conservatives in the week to March 29.
John Major's Conservatives have been dogged by a torrent of sleaze' allegations ranging from sex scandals to party members accused of accepting cash to put questions to parliament.
Carma said the bad press could have been a driving force behind Labour's opinion poll lead, as Blair was able to steal issues on which the Tories had hoped to shine.

The only bright spot of the Conservative campaign so far has been to raise the spectre of a return to 1970s-style trade union power under Labour, Spencer said. But Blair has hotly denied he can be manipulated by the unions.
Spencer said polls were clearly sensitive to newspapers and a shift in media sentiment could easily squeeze Labour's lead.

But with only a 4.5 percent swing in the vote needed for Labour to form the next government, the chances of even a blanket press conversion to the Tory cause sweeping them back in to power look wafer thin.
